Currently XWayland works like this for vsynced games:
1.  Flips get marked with [sync_flip](https://gitlab.freedesktop.org/xorg/xserver/blob/435d41d5ffe5467f43225b59411ca9f9a05c10a6/hw/xwayland/xwayland-present.c#L447).
1. On frame callback the MSC is [bumped](https://gitlab.freedesktop.org/xorg/xserver/blob/435d41d5ffe5467f43225b59411ca9f9a05c10a6/hw/xwayland/xwayland-present.c#L264).
1. The flip gets [marked](https://gitlab.freedesktop.org/xorg/xserver/blob/435d41d5ffe5467f43225b59411ca9f9a05c10a6/hw/xwayland/xwayland-present.c#L215) as done.

This has the following issue: The frame callback is not received by XWayland when the actual frame was presented but potentially later on when the compositor informs clients when there is ["a good time to start drawing the next one"](https://wayland.freedesktop.org/docs/html/apa.html#protocol-spec-wl_surface-request-frame).

I'm currently looking into replacing this with presentation-time protocol: [Task](https://gitlab.freedesktop.org/xorg/xserver/issues/971), [WIP-branch](https://gitlab.freedesktop.org/romangg/xserver/commits/presentation-time)

My current approach is in a first step to decouple XWayland frame stepping from the frame-callback completely and instead directly use the timing values received through presentation-time to drive with an internal timer the presentation (and realign the timer later on).

Second step would then be to maybe reintroduce the frame callback to throttle presenting when the surface is not visible (battery saving). But that depends on how much a difference this actually would make.

There are currently three issues I'm aware of:

### Cursor cap not respected
A notification window might end up on the cursor plane because the AMD driver does not check for cursor cap when doing an atomic test commit.

Simon has a patch for that on [the mailing list](https://lists.freedesktop.org/archives/amd-gfx/2020-March/047825.html). I had opened [a ticket](https://github.com/emersion/libliftoff/issues/46) for that issue some time ago in libliftoff. If the patch will be further stalled for kernel inclusion I would like to have the check in libliftoff instead.

### Layer properties mismatch
Properties on libliftoff layers are not "reset" when a layer is reallocated. This leads to sub-optimal or even broken allocations over time.

In our case the Steam overlay is blended in via the overlay alpha property. This alpha property is never kept afterwards with the same value on the libliftoff layer.

But I changed the code such that the alpha is only set when it is smaller 1 (otherwise the primary plane could never be used). That means if you blend out the Steam overlay and afterwards allocate a notification window to the overlay plane the notification will be invisible.

I had some ideas how to solve this issue in libliftoff but wanted to wait with formulating them out in the [issue ticket](https://github.com/emersion/libliftoff/issues/45) I created after Simon expressed some own thoughts about it. Since he is the maintainer and this could be a rather large change of the current architecture I thought I give him some time for developing a solution. But I will add some more details now.

An alternative solution right now for gamescope would be to reserve the first layer for the primary plane only and never set the alpha there. Have a second layer only for the overlay, always set the alpha there and a third layer potentially only for the cursor also never setting there the alpha. If the hardware supports more than one overlay a fourth can be used exclusively for notifications and without alpha.

### Missing fallback to composition layer
We currently don't use the compositing layer in case the allocation fails but recreate a new layer allocation.

See also here for some investigation in Arch Linux: https://bbs.archlinux.org/viewtopic.php?id=228032

Does Gamescope actually require your wlroots fork to be installed alongside it? Or is it merely a compile-time dependency?
No, wlroots doesn't need to be installed since gamescope statically links to it.

>so we're missing something to hold onto the game's buffer for as long as it's on screen maybe.

Yes. wlroots will send a `wl_buffer.release` event as soon as the game submits a new buffer. Compositors that need to hold on to the buffer for longer need to reference the buffer with `wlr_buffer_lock`.

This should only cause issues with direct scan-out though. Composition should work fine without `wlr_buffer_lock`.

Will investigate.

>This should only cause issues with direct scan-out though. Composition should work fine without wlr_buffer_lock.

Well, since threads are involved, scratch that.

OK - usually direct scanout is the preferred path in embedded so that would be consistent with what you initially said. Sounds like we'll want to lock the buffer until we have a replacement already scanned out or composited in all cases, then.

Does locking the buffer feed back into the WSI interfaces of the application at the other end? Eg. if we lock a buffer and all the other ones are busy, will the app's SwapBuffers() or AcquireNextImage() block until we unlock it?

>Does locking the buffer feed back into the WSI interfaces of the application at the other end? Eg. if we lock a buffer and all the other ones are busy, will the app's SwapBuffers() or AcquireNextImage() block until we unlock it?

Correct, clients can't start re-using the buffer before `wl_buffer.release`. See e.g. https://gitlab.freedesktop.org/mesa/mesa/-/blob/master/src/egl/drivers/dri2/platform_wayland.c#L238

A solution is to set WAYLAND_DISPLAY to something that isn't a socket. An empty string works well.

So this was all due to blitting in Xwayland - the current release uses a single intermediate buffer, so we were getting implicit-synced to oblivious. The infinite wait is when we get behind enough that we don't catch up to one frame faster than the game comes up with another one, which makes the one Xwayland buffer always busy as far as implicit sync is concerned.

Xwayland master addresses this issue by making multiple buffers as needed, and things look way better there.

In addition to that, there's some recent changes to avoid getting behind as much.

It's still abnormal to ever be blitting in Xwayland for our purposes, but we can track that as part of https://github.com/Plagman/gamescope/issues/21.

> before I try to wrap my head around it too much, was the simplification aimed to have exactly the same outcome in all exotic combinations of those flags?

Yes, that was the intent. The new logic sorts windows like so:

1. Sort windows with `gameID` set first
2. For all windows with `gameID` set, sort the ones which aren't override-redirect first
3. For all windows which aren't override-redirect, sort the ones with `wantsUnfocus` unset first
4. For all windows with `wantsUnfocus` unset, sort the ones with a greater `damage_sequence` first

The fact windows were previously picked from `vecPossibleFocusGameWindows` before `vecPossibleFocusAnyWindows` is now done via (1).  `allowNonGameOverrideRedirectWindow` and `usingOverrideRedirectWindow` are replaced by (2). The final `if ( focus->wantsUnfocus && vecPossibleFocusAnyWindows.size() >= 2 )` check is replaced with (3). The `if ( w->damage_sequence >= maxDamageSequence )` check is replaced by (4).

I now realize that the new logic doesn't re-implement _exactly_ the old one. Previously, non-game windows ignored `damage_sequence`, and game windows ignored `wantsUnfocus`. I can change the PR to do that if desirable, but not sure it really matters. For instance `wantsUnfocus` is set by a special steam property (I can't imagine it being wrongly set on a game window). Additionally `damage_sequence` was ignored by non-game widows, but is the last sorting criteria anyways (order was previously undefined for non-game windows with override-redirect unset and `wantsUnfocus` unset, with this PR gamescope will prefer windows in this category with a greater `damage_sequence`, so if anything that makes the focus logic more predictable).

This PR implements the "focus score" we've been discussing in the past, except without an explicit score. This makes it easier to tweak the ordering: instead of fine-tuning weights for each criteria, we can just change the priorities in the sort function.

Adding more trace points, it seems like Xwayland is committing a buffer right after we request it:

- t=0ms: gamescope calls `paint_all`
- t=0.12ms: gamescope sends a `wl_surface.frame` event to Xwayland, requesting a new commit
- t=0.20ms: the vulkan WSI in the sekiro process sends a `Present` request to display a new frame
- t=0.55ms: gamescope receives the `wl_surface.commit` event with the new frame

- wlroots with the headless backend and EGL renderer
- Vulkan
- DRM

As such, I only have two options with `flatpak-builder` for working around `stb` using git-wrap:
1. Add a buildsystem and `.pc` file to `stb` in a downstream patch so it would become installable and discoverable by buildsystems. Then build it as its own git module and let `gamescope` discover it during build.
2. Covert `stb` back to a git submodule using a downstream git repository for `gamescope`. Using a downstream patch is not even possible because `flatpak-builder` runs `git submodule update --init` after checkout and before any patches are applied. This means patches cannot add or remove submodules.

Maintaining a downstream patch for `stb` is not reasonable, and upstream will never accept it as they wish to remain non-installable. Simiarly, maintaining a downstream git repository for `gamescope` is not a reasonable expectation from downstream packagers, and breaks automatic update discovery (i.e., `flatpak-external-data-checker`).

Not only flatpak-builder on Flathub disallows network access at build time, this is common for most linux package build systems.  E.g. Fedora as well will have hard time updating gamescope in their repos, and will have to use some workaround, too. 
Offline builds are essential for reproducibility, since there is no way to ensure a build can be reproduced if it can download arbitrary files at build time.

But if you want to use meson wrap files instead of git submodules, you could provide release tarballs (generated using `meson dist --include-subprojects`) to help packaging the program.

Right, I mentioned reproducibility above:
> for enforcing build isolation sanity, not preparation sanity -- you want to catch build systems doing weird ***and unreproducible*** things.

Some linux distros do enforce network isolation -- I strongly hesitate to call that consistent, and some of the distros that do have it make it optional (for example Gentoo). Other ecosystems, like Debian, don't use distfiles at all, but reprocess your source code to strip out the bits they don't like, add in bits they do like, and recompress your source code using their preferred compression algorithm. They will just update the subprojects on the developer's machine and upload a debian source package which has it included... I believe redhat does something similar with a global side cache of distfiles, which under rare circumstances actually do get modified for legal reasons...

It almost has to be optional for practical reasons, because cursed languages like npm don't work without it (if only we could just reject the language and anything written using it, eh?) and partially cursed languages like golang and rust mostly don't work without it but do have subcommands, like meson, to create an offline cache.

The correct solution is indeed `meson dist --include-subprojects`.

Or only using dependencies that are packaged by distros (header-only libraries that upstream refuses to make packageable need not apply). And leave subprojects to be used as convenience mechanisms for optionally vendoring system dependencies, which never gets in the way of distros or flatpak-builder.

Given neither of those currently apply here, running preparatory steps with network enabled isn't an unreasonable workaround (but I will still be fixing `meson subprojects update --reset` to gracefully continue if the git clone already exists but network failures prevent fetching updates.

There are several different approaches to making this work, most of which work today, and the very last place I ever want to point fingers at, myself, is "this is using meson subprojects correctly and should stop".

The initial version of this series used a shared memory as a mean to synchronize two processes: gamescope would set a flag which would then be detected and cleared on mangoapp (a standalone version of the mangohud). Frame time would be computed on the mangoapp side, based when it would detect a change in flag.

This version had some drawbacks: 1. the scheduler would be impacting the reported fps; 2. Some frames may not be detected (the SHM pointer wasn't marked as volatile, and the mango app may not be scheduled fast enough); 3. having the mangoapp busy-loop is a waste of CPU resources.

To address these issues, I switched to a System V message queue (roughly the same concepts as the POSIX one). This allows gamescope to push a list of frame times to mangoapp, which is then free to process and re-draw at its earlier convenience.

Finally, the message structured has been defined to make it both backwards and forwards compatible, allowing updates to mangoapp and gamescope to be performed independently. This is achieved via versioning of the messages, and using an append-only approach after that to detect which fields are present or not based on the message size.

The issue here isn't the shortcut keys but the modifier behavior. If you run an application under Gamescope that understands the modifier key by itself (like, e.g. virtualbox, 86box/pcem or parsec that then has Windows as a guest or at the other side), the event for pressing the modifier is passed on and handled but then once the modifier key is released together with the rest of the shortcut (e.g. F for Super+F), the event for the release isn't passed on.

Changing the shortcut keys wouldn't really change much since, e.g., if one used Ctrl+F you'd have Ctrl being sent to the underlying program (so in many shooters you'd shoot before F is also pressed).

Since one can't really hold down the two keys immediately the only way to avoid this is to block the modifier key events completely. This is also what virtualbox is doing with its "host" key (it uses right control as the modifier instead of the super key, but the idea is the same).

I have a strong suspicion that this is related to synchronization missing somewhere. I already saw similar noise patterns in an unrelated project where rendering was done to a GBM buffer, which afterwards was 1) encoded into a video stream using Intel MSDK, and 2) was presented on the screen in a Weston compositor. Overall looks okay, but:

1. The modifiers will be incorrect (e.g. no shift when typing uppercase letters…)
2. I'd prefer an approach where we re-use the default en-US keymap
We don't support modifiers at all in this path, so I figured this was the best compromise.

The point is:

- Good X11 clients shouldn't interpret raw keycodes, the keycodes don't mean anything without a keymap
- This patch makes it so raw keycodes look a bit more like what would happen with a "real" physical keyboard, but
- This patch doesn't completely make ASCII characters look like what would happen with a "real" physical keyboard, because e.g. uppercase letters and special characters won't be recognized correctly by bad X11 clients

So I wonder what this patch really fixes? Do you have an example game which behaves better with this applied?

Maybe it makes more sense to rework the way the scratch cmd buffer stuff works.
I don't think we need such a ridiculous amount anymore now that we de-duplicate incoming commits with the `wlr_buffer_map`.

Previously, it was designed so that every incoming commit would get its own buffer so it didn't stall, even at high fps, but now, we de-duplicate those incoming commits, so that's less of an issue... Unless it's stupid xwayland blitting which is unbounded :(((((((((((

Perhaps just raising the FD limit is good enough for now, until we solve the unbounded commits coming from xwayland blits. We need to solve that to implement the FPS limiter/vsync replacement the way we want to anyway.

Does NVIDIA intend to support `GAMMA_LUT` in future?
We use this to implement Night Mode.

Additionally, perhaps it makes sense for the NVIDIA driver to not make/expose an fd without `VK_KHR_external_fence_fd`.

However if this is instead an implementation detail, I would understand that is not possible :b
Yes there was a regression, but it was already fixed in the next release. 3.11.22 is pretty old.

Support for GAMMA_LUT is in the queue, but no ETA at the moment.

We currently need the FD regardless of fence import/export as part of our internal implementation. Using fewer fences would be great if that's an option in the future. Raising the limit seems pretty harmless in the meantime though.

Does this have to be a *Windows* non-Steam game via Proton, or does the Steam Deck branch of Steam use pressure-vessel for native Linux games too? My understanding was that native Linux non-Steam games do not normally use pressure-vessel.

> Steam Flatpak messing with the process tree in this way seems like the real issue here.

There is no alternative to this. Flatpak apps are not allowed to create new user namespaces "below" the Flatpak sandbox, only in parallel, because if they could create new user namespaces, then they would be able to use that for a sandbox escape similar to CVE-2021-41133.

> Does killing games, and using Steam Input, other Steam API features even work in Steam Flatpak in non-Steam games because of this?..

Killing games is special-cased for this arrangement: instead of immediately sending `SIGKILL` to the `reaper` and its children, Steam sends a `SIGTERM` to the `pressure-vessel-launch` process (or `steam-runtime-launch-client` in recent betas), which results in it communicating with `flatpak-portal` and asking it to send `SIGTERM` to `pressure-vessel-adverb`. The adverb (which is a subreaper, like Steam's `reaper`) sends `SIGTERM` to child processes, waits a short time for them to exit, and sends `SIGKILL` to any survivors.

I believe Steam Input also works.

pressure-vessel could wrap the Flatpak subsandbox in a `reaper` process if that would help, although it would still need to use `pressure-vessel-adverb` as a subreaper to get the process-killing behaviour.

How does Steam communicate for IPC if its in a separate sandbox?

It depends on the type of IPC in use (there are lots, and they interact with namespaces differently), but in general the answer is that Flatpak is instructed to share the IPC mechanism between the original sandbox (the one with the Steam client) and the subsandbox (the one with the game).

For `kill()` and similar process-ID-oriented mechanisms, flatpak/flatpak#4060 added an option to share the pid namespace between the Steam client and the subsandbox, and we use it.

For SysV IPC (semaphores and message queues), the Steam Flatpak app has `--share=ipc`, so the Steam client and the subsandbox both share the IPC namespace with the host system.

For filesystem-backed mechanisms (shared memory, AF_UNIX sockets, or pipes), flatpak/flatpak#4120, flatpak/flatpak#4093 and flatpak/flatpak#4124 share `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR`, `/tmp` and `/dev/shm` (respectively) between the Steam client and the subsandbox. The subsandbox also shares `~/.steam` with the Steam client (pressure-vessel does not attempt to put a security boundary between Steam and games).

Abstract AF_UNIX sockets are part of the network namespace, and Steam has `--share=net`, so the Steam client and the subsandbox both share abstract AF_UNIX sockets with the host.

As far as I can tell, the non-Steam game AppId detection in `gamescope` looks at the command line used to execute its anscestor `reaper` process, presumably because there's no "sane" way to obtain the AppId in this case (yet?). Here's an example of such a command line, from my tests:
```
/home/dor/.var/app/com.valvesoftware.Steam/.local/share/Steam/ubuntu12_32/reaper SteamLaunch AppId=2929382885 -- /media/storage/SteamLibrary/steamapps/common/SteamLinuxRuntime_soldier/_v2-entry-point --verb=waitforexitandrun -- /media/storage/SteamLibrary/steamapps/common/SteamLinuxRuntime/scout-on-soldier-entry-point-v2 -- /media/storage/SteamExternal/glxgears/glxgears
```
Spawning an appropriate `reaper` process inside the subsandbox would indeed solve the issue. However, it must similarly have the "AppId" command line argument like the original for `gamescope`'s logic to work. Generally, it may be best to have `pressure-vessel` pass the exact same command-line arguments to its reaper process as was passed to the original. For example, in the case above, like so: `path/to/reaper SteamLaunch AppId=2929382885 -- ...`.

Are you guys sure you wanted to use `-W 1920 -H 1080 -w 3840 -h 2160` instead of `-W 3840 -H 2160 -w 1920 -h 1080`?

The first would run present a resolution of 3840x2160 to the game which may render at a lower resolution, then upscale to 4k (or in this case, glxgears rendering natively to 4k without upscaling), then gamescope downscales that again to FHD, finally upscaling it back to your screen. This sounds very inefficient.

It works fine the other way around, letting gamescope upscale with FSR if you also use `-U`. The lower case resolution letters are what the nested client sees as the resolution.

Quick update: I was able to track down the issue in the driver and write up a fix. I misunderstood the comment above as I assumed it was data collected on a Pascal-class GPU. The problem is actually that Vulkan doesn't advertise compressed DRM format modifiers, which means Gamescope doesn't either, which means Xwayland also doesn't when running on Gamescope, which in turn confuses our GLX driver when running on this configuration, as it was expecting both compressed and uncompressed modifiers to be available when running on Xwayland.

Thanks again for the help from the community in debugging this issue.

> Quick update: I was able to track down the issue in the driver and write up a fix. I misunderstood the comment above as I assumed it was data collected on a Pascal-class GPU. The problem is actually that Vulkan doesn't advertise compressed DRM format modifiers, which means Gamescope doesn't either, which means Xwayland also doesn't when running on Gamescope, which in turn confuses our GLX driver when running on this configuration, as it was expecting both compressed and uncompressed modifiers to be available when running on Xwayland.

> Thanks again for the help from the community in debugging this issue.

Now run try to compile again.

If I understand correctly, this patch is meant to work around gamescope thinking the display is always rotated by 270°, which fails when display is mounted at 90° angle.

Why wasn't KMS panel orientation property used? It looks like the proper solution that will(as long as devices are added to [Linux's built-in panel orientation quirks](https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/master/drivers/gpu/drm/drm_panel_orientation_quirks.c).
Of course, devices needing rotation will need to be added to this, but in the long run it will end up saving a lot of time, instead of having for every user of gamescope to experiment with rotation or have the packager of gamescope guess rotation of devices.

This will affect all users of a given device, with alternatives being inconvenient/unusable(who holds their gaming handhelds vertically or upside down?).

I think using KMS panel orientation property will end up with much nicer user experience, less time spent packaging overall and will have more devices added automatically(as long as kernel is being updated).

If the command line option is absolutely required, maybe let's just add both rotation deriving from KMS panel orientation, and if the `--force-orientation` option is specified use that.

https://github.com/Plagman/gamescope/commit/cce6a29a2494eaf8f99e299a39b957fda3fcdb2a checks whether the client does this:

```
wl_surface@1.attach(buffer@2)
wl_surface@1.commit() # commit A
wl_surface@1.commit() # commit B
```

In commit B, the client hasn't attached a new buffer, and the flag check makes us skip the commit.

In the situation handled by this PR, the client does this:

```
wl_surface@1.attach(buffer@2)
wl_surface@1.commit() # commit A
wl_surface@1.attach(buffer@2)
wl_surface@1.commit() # commit B
```

In that case, the flag will be set, and we won't skip the commit.

Ok. Following @ruineka lead I came to the conclusion that something changed in the kernel behaviour that makes https://github.com/Plagman/gamescope/blob/0626c7c8f8afdb95c1aa82111922f3da74ec9996/src/steamcompmgr.cpp#L1914 return non-zero.

Aside from that, the other thing I discovered is that drm_set_mode() only sets `g_DRM->pending.mode_id = mode` and also sets `needs_modeset = true` triggering some properties setting inside `drm_prepare()` but the check in https://github.com/Plagman/gamescope/blob/0626c7c8f8afdb95c1aa82111922f3da74ec9996/src/steamcompmgr.cpp#L1922 checks for `g_DRM->current.mode_id` instead. `drm_prepare()` never sets `current.mode_id` so that will always be zero until `drm_commit()` is called and copies `drm->current = drm->pending` if the commit succeded.

According to the message in https://github.com/Plagman/gamescope/blob/0626c7c8f8afdb95c1aa82111922f3da74ec9996/src/steamcompmgr.cpp#L1924 the modeset fails, but is checking the wrong variable. So I can think of two solutions:
- Set `drm->current.mode_id = drm->pending.mode_id` when the property is correctly set by `drm_prepare()` below line https://github.com/Plagman/gamescope/blob/0626c7c8f8afdb95c1aa82111922f3da74ec9996/src/drm.cpp#L1716
- Check for both `g_DRM->current.mode_id == 0 && g_DRM->pending.mode_id == 0` in line https://github.com/Plagman/gamescope/blob/0626c7c8f8afdb95c1aa82111922f3da74ec9996/src/steamcompmgr.cpp#L1922
so the message is correct (we don´t have a mode nor a pending one and mode setting did fail).

Both were tested and work without breaking anything (as far as I tested). The thing is, that the next if statement is also triggered ("failed to prepare 1-layer flip") but is harmless and only happens once.

I can prepare any of the solutions above, but I'm not entirely sure is a propper fix.

Root cause, confirmed on RTX 3090, NVIDIA 615.78.08 (open kernel modules), Xwayland 24.1.15, gamescope 3.17.0, nested in Hyprland:

Steam's webhelper logs `ThreadInit: GLX_EXT_texture_from_pixmap extension unavailable` → `Falling back to system composer`. That fallback draws the overlays (side menu, notifications, Home over a running game) on opaque windows, hence the black boxes.

`glxinfo` on Xwayland shows `GLX_EXT_texture_from_pixmap` in both the *server* GLX extensions (vendor "SGI", Xwayland's GLX) and the *client* GLX extensions (vendor "NVIDIA Corporation"), but **not** in the effective "GLX extensions" list. libGLX_nvidia drops it when the server is Xwayland. Same result outside gamescope (Hyprland's Xwayland), so it isn't gamescope.

Whats needed implement it already work on this driver: Xwayland returns the window's buffer via DRI3 `BuffersFromPixmap` (NVIDIA modifier 0x300000000606014), NVIDIA Vulkan imports it, and NVIDIA EGL has `EGL_EXT_image_dma_buf_import(_modifiers)`. EGPU-Buddy's shim (https://github.com/denver8989/EGPU-Buddy, packaging/steam-ui-fix) uses that path to provide the extension to steamwebhelper (DRI3 buffer → Vulkan copy → GL texture via GL_EXT_memory_object_fd). With it preloaded, Steam's GL compositor starts and the overlays are transparent again.

What would fix it:
- NVIDIA: expose GLX_EXT_texture_from_pixmap in libGLX_nvidia under Xwayland, implemented via DRI3 BuffersFromPixmap + dmabuf import.
- Valve (Steam client), as a workaround: when the extension is missing, import window pixmaps via DRI3 + EGL_EXT_image_dma_buf_import instead of falling back to the opaque system composer.

<details><summary>Additional reproduction: HDR enabled on an external monitor causes washed-out colours on an internal SDR display</summary>

I have reproduced what appears to be this issue on an ONEXPLAYER X1 Pro running Bazzite GNOME. The distinguishing factor in my case is that the display affected by the incorrect colour transformations is not the display on which HDR was enabled.

### Environment

- Device: ONEXPLAYER X1 Pro
- APU: AMD Ryzen AI 9 HX 370
- GPU: AMD Radeon 890M (1002:150e)
- OS: Bazzite Deck GNOME 45.20261125
- Kernel: 7.3.5-ogc3.1.fc45.x86_64
- Gamescope: 3.17.0-ogc1+
- Mutter: 51.1
- GNOME Shell: 51.1
- AMD Display Core: 3.2.392 (DCN 3.5)
- Internal display: BOE YHB0AP23 (eDP-1), 2560x1600 @ 120Hz, SDR
- External display: Samsung LS34A650U (DP-2), 3440x1440 @ 100Hz, HDR capable

### Steps to reproduce

1. Connect the external monitor before booting.
2. Boot directly into Gamescope Gaming Mode.
3. Ensure HDR and full colour range are enabled on the external monitor.
4. Gaming Mode outputs exclusively to the external monitor. The internal display is disabled.
5. Switch to GNOME Desktop Mode, where both displays are enabled and HDR is disabled.

### Actual behaviour

The internal SDR display becomes significantly washed out, with elevated black levels, reduced contrast and a purple-grey tint. The external monitor displays colours correctly.

Screenshots captured through GNOME appear normal. The issue is visible in photographs of the physical display and persists when switching to a text-only TTY.

### Expected behaviour

Both displays should output correct SDR colours after switching to Desktop Mode, irrespective of the HDR configuration used in Gamescope.

### DRM diagnostic comparison

I captured DRM properties using drm_info under three conditions:

- **Working:** Boot with the external monitor disconnected, switch to Desktop Mode, then connect the external monitor.
- **Broken:** Boot with the external monitor connected and HDR enabled in Gaming Mode, then switch to Desktop Mode.
- **Recovered:** Return to Gaming Mode, disable HDR on the external monitor, then return to Desktop Mode without rebooting.

Both the working and broken captures were taken using the same kernel and Bazzite deployment.

The internal display is assigned to connector 143, CRTC 123 and primary plane 83 in both captures.

| Property | Working | Broken |
|---|---|---|
| AMD_PLANE_DEGAMMA_TF | sRGB EOTF | sRGB EOTF |
| AMD_PLANE_SHAPER_TF | sRGB inv_EOTF | sRGB inv_EOTF |
| AMD_PLANE_BLEND_TF | sRGB EOTF | PQ EOTF |
| AMD_CRTC_REGAMMA_TF | sRGB inv_EOTF | PQ inv_EOTF |
| AMD_PLANE_HDR_MULT | 4294967296 | 4294967296 |
| HDR_OUTPUT_METADATA | 0 | 0 |
| Colorspace | Default | Default |
| DEGAMMA_LUT | 0 | 0 |
| CTM | 0 | 0 |

AMD_PLANE_SHAPER_LUT and AMD_PLANE_LUT3D are populated in both states, although their blob IDs differ. I have not compared the underlying LUT contents.

The significant differences are AMD_PLANE_BLEND_TF and AMD_CRTC_REGAMMA_TF, which retain PQ transfer functions in the broken SDR desktop session.

The external monitor's corresponding transfer functions remain at Default in both desktop captures.

### Gamescope journal evidence

During the working boot:

    drm: selecting connector eDP-1
    drm: selecting mode 1600x2560@120Hz
    server hdr output enabled: false

During the broken boot:

    drm: selecting connector DP-2
    drm: selecting mode 3440x1440@100Hz
    xwm: HDR output enabled

After switching to GNOME, both connectors report HDR_OUTPUT_METADATA = 0, but the AMD-specific transfer functions on the internal display remain configured for PQ.

### Confirmed recovery without rebooting

1. Return to Gaming Mode.
2. Disable HDR on the external monitor.
3. Leave full colour range enabled.
4. Return to Desktop Mode.

The internal display immediately returns to correct colours.

A subsequent drm_info capture confirms that:

- AMD_PLANE_BLEND_TF returns to sRGB EOTF.
- AMD_CRTC_REGAMMA_TF returns to sRGB inv_EOTF.
- No plane or CRTC reports an active PQ transfer function.

### Other diagnostic tests

The following made no visible difference while the issue was present:

- Disabling the internal display's ICC colour profile.
- Forcing full RGB range through GNOME.
- Changing the internal display refresh rate between 60Hz and 120Hz.
- Switching to a text-only TTY.

AMDGPU panel power savings was already disabled.

### Conclusion

The evidence suggests that AMD-private DRM colour-management properties configured during the Gamescope HDR session are retained across the compositor handover.

Of particular interest is that the affected internal display was disabled during Gaming Mode, while HDR was active exclusively on the external display.

Disabling HDR in Gamescope restores the expected transfer functions and resolves the issue without rebooting.

I have not established whether the responsibility for resetting these properties lies with Gamescope, AMDGPU or the incoming compositor.

Related Bazzite issue: https://github.com/ublue-os/bazzite/issues/2091

Another data point, this time the **reverse topology** of the laptops above: an AMD **desktop** where the display is on the *discrete* GPU and the iGPU has no display at all. Same root cause as discussed here (gamescope's DRM backend ends up on a Vulkan device that has no connected connector), but with an extra trigger that may help.

**Setup:** Ryzen 7 9800X3D (iGPU, Raphael) + RX 9070 XT, TV connected directly to the dGPU's HDMI port. Bazzite, gamescope `3.17.0-ogc1+`, `gamescope-session-plus`.

**The GPU gamescope picks depends on whether a display is connected at boot:**

| Boot | Display at boot | Vulkan device picked | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | HDMI connected | `RX 9070 XT (RADV GFX1201)` | `selecting connector HDMI-A-1`, works |
| B | no HDMI cable | `Ryzen 7 9800X3D (RADV RAPHAEL_MENDOCINO)` | `drm: cannot find any connected connector!` |

Case B:

```
vulkan: selecting physical device 'AMD Ryzen 7 9800X3D 8-Core Processor (RADV RAPHAEL_MENDOCINO)'
wlserver: [backend/headless/backend.c:60] Creating headless backend
drm: opening DRM node '/dev/dri/card1'
drm: cannot find any connected connector!
```

(The `cardN` numbers of the two GPUs swap between boots, so the node name alone is not a reliable hint.)

It does not crash here: gamescope stays alive on the headless backend. But it **never recovers**. Plugging the HDMI cable in afterwards (the kernel then reports `HDMI-A-1: connected`) does nothing, and restarting the session with the cable already connected picks the iGPU again. Only a reboot with the cable attached fixed it. I don't know why it prefers the iGPU when nothing is connected; that part is unverified.

**Workaround confirmed (as suggested earlier in this thread):** `--prefer-vk-device 1002:7550` (the dGPU). On Bazzite the session script reads `~/.config/environment.d/*.conf`, so `VULKAN_ADAPTER=1002:7550` is enough. With it, a boot **without** the cable selects the RX 9070 XT, stays up on the headless backend (no crash, no coredump), and when I plug the cable in afterwards it switches to the real connector by itself:

```
drm: Connector HDMI-A-1 -> ...
drm: selecting connector HDMI-A-1
drm: selecting mode 3840x2160@60Hz
xwm: HDR output enabled
```

Tested once, on one machine. #1220 and #611 mention a SIGSEGV when `--prefer-vk-device` points at a dGPU with no connected output; I did not hit it here.

Suggestion: when no connector is connected on the chosen device, gamescope could try other DRM devices (or keep probing all of them on hotplug) instead of settling on the first/iGPU device, rather than requiring users to pin a GPU by hand.

The same machine is also reported against SteamOS at https://github.com/ValveSoftware/SteamOS/issues/2839 (same signature, different distro).
